claims.text: An ultrathin coherent Nb interlayer can mediate a transition from diffusion-dominated creep to dislocation-mediated creep in HEA multilayers.
The initial HEA multilayers have coherent interfaces.
Coherent interfaces in the initial HEA multilayers favor diffusion-mediated creep at elevated temperatures.
The proposed Nb interlayer is nanometric and thinner than 10 nm.
Creep is active under mechanical loading in the proposed temperature range of 600–900 °C.
An HEA/Nb boundary modifies interface coherency.
Modified coherency at the HEA/Nb boundary alters dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Nb has an intermediate lattice parameter relative to typical HEAs.
Nb has an intermediate diffusivity relative to typical HEAs.
A coherent Nb interlayer maintains good atomic bonding.
A coherent Nb interlayer perturbs local diffusion paths.
Increasing temperature slightly relaxes coherency at the HEA/Nb interface.
Relaxed HEA/Nb interface coherency facilitates dislocation nucleation and glide.
Enhanced dislocation nucleation and glide reduce the predominance of diffusion creep and shift deformation toward dislocation-mediated creep.
The Nb interlayer will reduce the overall high-temperature creep rate relative to an HEA multilayer without Nb.
The Nb interlayer will increase dislocation activity relative to diffusion-dominated deformation in the baseline multilayer.
Baseline HEA multilayers without Nb are primarily governed by diffusion-mediated creep at high temperature.
The beneficial effect is limited to few-nanometer Nb layers that preserve overall interface coherence.
Excessive Nb thickness or processing-induced incoherency may eliminate the proposed creep-mechanism transition.
The optimal Nb thickness, effective temperature range, and magnitude of mechanism modification depend on HEA composition and processing history.
